items.stem: Define the term 'full costing'.
items.answer: A costing method in which all indirect costs (overheads) are allocated to products or cost centres, so each product bears a share of total costs.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, a costing method in which all indirect costs (overheads) are allocated to products or cost centres, so each product bears a share of total costs. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a product that makes a loss under full costing may still be worth keeping.
items.answer: If it has a positive contribution, it covers its variable costs and helps pay fixed costs, which would still have to be paid if it were dropped.
items.markingKey: 1 mark positive contribution; 1 mark fixed costs remain. [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of full costing.
items.answer: Advantage: all costs are covered, useful for setting prices. Disadvantage: overhead allocation is arbitrary and may distort product profitability.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each with explanation. [2]

items.stem: Based in Lima, Andes Textil SA (family-owned private company) makes premium alpaca knitwear for fashion retailers in North America and Japan. The business has around 320 employees. The founder is retiring and the new managing director wants to modernise production. Explain why the way Andes Textil allocates overheads could affect its pricing decisions.
items.answer: Points to develop for Andes Textil: full costing allocates overheads to products; different bases (floor space, labour hours) give different costs; over-costed products may be priced too high; under-costed products may seem more profitable than they are.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: full costing allocates overheads to products. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Andes Textil: textile manufacturing, about 320 employees, family-owned private company in Peru; the founder is retiring and the new managing director wants to modernise production). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Andes Textil, e.g. different bases (floor space, labour hours) give different costs; over-costed products may be priced too high; under-costed products may seem more profitable than they are. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Many young workers are leaving the estates for jobs in the cities. Lanka Tea Estates plc, a public limited company in Sri Lanka with about 5,000 employees, grows, processes and packs tea on its own estates. Explain how Lanka Tea could use contribution costing to decide which product lines to keep.
items.answer: Points to develop for Lanka Tea: contribution = revenue − variable costs; products with positive contribution help cover fixed costs; dropping such products would reduce total profit; consider spare capacity and links between products.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: contribution = revenue − variable costs. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Lanka Tea: agriculture and food, about 5,000 employees, public limited company in Sri Lanka; many young workers are leaving the estates for jobs in the cities). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Lanka Tea, e.g. products with positive contribution help cover fixed costs; dropping such products would reduce total profit; consider spare capacity and links between products. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Occupancy rates have fallen since two new rival hotels opened nearby. Desert Bloom Hotels plc, a public limited company in the United Arab Emirates with about 3,100 employees, operates fourteen four- and five-star hotels. Evaluate whether Desert Bloom should stop producing a product that shows a loss under full costing.
items.answer: For: loss-making on full cost; resources could go to more profitable lines; simpler range. Against: positive contribution helps pay fixed costs; complementary sales may be lost; fixed costs remain after closure. Judgement: the decision for Desert Bloom depends mainly on the contribution of the product, and also on alternative uses of capacity.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [2]: uses case evidence (Desert Bloom: hospitality, about 3,100 employees, public limited company in the United Arab Emirates; occupancy rates have fallen since two new rival hotels opened nearby). AO3 Analysis [4]: arguments for, e.g. loss-making on full cost; resources could go to more profitable lines; simpler range; arguments against, e.g. positive contribution helps pay fixed costs; complementary sales may be lost; fixed costs remain after closure. AO4 Evaluation [4]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on the contribution of the product; alternative uses of capacity; effect on customers and brand. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Desert Bloom, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: Under full costing, overheads are allocated to products
options: according to their selling price only
on a chosen basis such as floor space or labour hours
only to the most profitable product
items.answer: on a chosen basis such as floor space or labour hours
items.markingKey: on a chosen basis such as floor space or labour hours. Full costing apportions indirect costs using an allocation basis.

items.stem: A rival in China has started selling machine-made balls at lower prices. Indus Sports Goods Ltd, a private limited company in Pakistan with about 950 employees, makes hand-stitched and machine-stitched footballs and cricket equipment. Explain one disadvantage to Indus Sports of using contribution costing rather than full costing for product decisions.
items.answer: Fixed costs may be ignored in pricing.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant disadvantage, e.g. fixed costs may be ignored in pricing; long-run prices must cover all costs; variable/fixed split may be unclear. 1 mark: explained in the context of Indus Sports (sports equipment manufacturing). [2]

items.stem: Explain why contribution costing is useful for short-term decisions.
items.answer: It separates fixed and variable costs, showing how profit changes when output, prices or product mix change, without arbitrary overhead allocation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark separates variable/fixed; 1 mark decision use. [2]

items.stem: BatikPay Sdn Bhd makes three products — Product X: 8,000 units at $40, variable cost $28 per unit, floor space 60%; Product Y: 4,000 units at $30, variable cost $18 per unit, floor space 25%; Product Z: 5,000 units at $20, variable cost $10 per unit, floor space 15%. Fixed overheads of $100,000 are allocated by floor space. Calculate the total contribution of each product.

Based in Seoul, Han River Games Co. (private limited company) develops mobile games that earn revenue from in-game purchases. The business has around 340 employees. One game earns 70% of its revenue and its popularity is starting to fall. Explain why the way Han River Games allocates overheads could affect its pricing decisions.
items.answer: Points to develop for Han River Games: full costing allocates overheads to products; different bases (floor space, labour hours) give different costs; over-costed products may be priced too high; under-costed products may seem more profitable than they are.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: full costing allocates overheads to products. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Han River Games: video game development, about 340 employees, private limited company in South Korea; one game earns 70% of its revenue and its popularity is starting to fall). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Han River Games, e.g. different bases (floor space, labour hours) give different costs; over-costed products may be priced too high; under-costed products may seem more profitable than they are. items.stem: Based in Doha, Pearl Logistics WLL (private limited company) provides freight forwarding, warehousing and lorry delivery services. The business has around 1,500 employees. Large customers are asking for real-time tracking of every delivery. (a) Define 'full costing'. (b) Explain one advantage to Pearl Logistics of using contribution costing rather than full costing for product decisions.
items.answer: (a) A costing method in which all indirect costs (overheads) are allocated to products or cost centres, so each product bears a share of total costs. (b) Avoids arbitrary overhead allocation.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark partial, 2 marks full definition [2] (b) 1 mark point (avoids arbitrary overhead allocation; shows each product's contribution to fixed costs; useful for special orders and product mix), 1 mark explanation, 1 mark application to Pearl Logistics [3]

items.stem: Define the term 'special order'.
items.answer: A one-off order from a customer, often at a lower price than normal, which the business must decide whether to accept.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, a one-off order from a customer, often at a lower price than normal, which the business must decide whether to accept. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a business might accept a special order at a price below full cost.
items.answer: With spare capacity, fixed costs are already paid, so any price above variable cost gives extra contribution and increases profit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark fixed costs already covered; 1 mark positive contribution. [2]

items.stem: Explain two non-financial factors to consider when deciding whether to accept a special order.
items.answer: Reaction of existing customers to a lower price; possibility of future orders; effect on brand image; pressure on staff and capacity.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark factor, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Based in Singapore, Lumen Robotics plc (public limited company) designs and builds robots used on factory assembly lines. The business has around 2,400 employees. Shareholders are pressing for higher dividends while engineers want more spending on research. Explain why Lumen Robotics might reject a special order that offers a positive contribution.
items.answer: Points to develop for Lumen Robotics: positive contribution adds profit only if capacity is spare; displaced regular sales may be more profitable; damage to price perception and brand; stress on staff and quality.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: positive contribution adds profit only if capacity is spare. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Lumen Robotics: industrial engineering, about 2,400 employees, public limited company in Singapore; shareholders are pressing for higher dividends while engineers want more spending on research). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Lumen Robotics, e.g. displaced regular sales may be more profitable; damage to price perception and brand; stress on staff and quality. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.answer: Points to develop for Desert Bloom: contribution: price compared with variable cost; spare capacity and opportunity cost; reaction of existing customers; future business and payment risk.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: contribution: price compared with variable cost. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Desert Bloom: hospitality, about 3,100 employees, public limited company in the United Arab Emirates; occupancy rates have fallen since two new rival hotels opened nearby). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Desert Bloom, e.g. spare capacity and opportunity cost; reaction of existing customers; future business and payment risk. items.answer: Points to develop for Gold Coast Cocoa: positive contribution adds profit only if capacity is spare; displaced regular sales may be more profitable; damage to price perception and brand; stress on staff and quality.

items.stem: Lagos Bites Ltd is a private limited company based in Lagos, Nigeria. It produces packaged snacks such as plantain chips and chin chin and employs about 700 people. Rising costs of imported packaging have cut its profit margins. Evaluate whether Lagos Bites should accept a special order at a price 20% below its normal price.
items.answer: For: positive contribution; uses spare capacity; potential long-term customer. Against: existing customers may demand discounts; capacity may be needed for regular sales; quality and delivery risks. Judgement: the decision for Lagos Bites depends mainly on the amount of spare capacity, and also on whether the markets can be kept separate.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [2]: uses case evidence (Lagos Bites: food processing, about 700 employees, private limited company in Nigeria; rising costs of imported packaging have cut its profit margins). AO4 Evaluation [4]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on the amount of spare capacity; whether the markets can be kept separate; the strategic value of the customer. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Lagos Bites, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: A major US retailer has asked it to cut delivery times from twelve weeks to six. Mekong Furniture JSC, a joint stock company in Vietnam with about 1,200 employees, makes wooden and rattan furniture for large retailers in the USA and Europe. Discuss whether contribution analysis alone should decide whether Mekong Furniture accepts special orders.
items.answer: For: clear financial result; easy to calculate; shows short-term profit effect. Against: ignores customer reactions and brand; ignores long-term relationships; assumes costs are accurate. Judgement: the decision for Mekong Furniture depends mainly on its capacity position, and also on its pricing strategy.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [3]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [3]: uses case evidence (Mekong Furniture: furniture manufacturing, about 1,200 employees, joint stock company in Vietnam; a major US retailer has asked it to cut delivery times from twelve weeks to six). AO3 Analysis [5]: arguments for, e.g. clear financial result; easy to calculate; shows short-term profit effect; arguments against, e.g. ignores customer reactions and brand; ignores long-term relationships; assumes costs are accurate. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Mekong Furniture, not a generic one. [16]

items.stem: Which business term is described here: "The difference between the maximum output a business can produce and its current output."
items.answer: spare capacity
items.markingKey: This is the definition of spare capacity.

items.stem: Bookings are highly seasonal and most guides are employed only for the summer. Kiwi Trails Ltd, a private limited company in New Zealand with about 90 employees, runs guided hiking, kayaking and cycling tours. Explain one advantage to Kiwi Trails of accepting a large special order at a discounted price.
items.answer: Extra contribution and profit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant advantage, e.g. extra contribution and profit; uses spare capacity; possible repeat business and new market. 1 mark: explained in the context of Kiwi Trails (tourism). [2]

items.stem: Explain why the opportunity cost of a special order is zero only when there is spare capacity.
items.answer: With spare capacity nothing else is given up; at full capacity normal sales must be lost, so their contribution is the opportunity cost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark spare capacity; 1 mark displaced sales. [2]

items.stem: A business with spare capacity is offered an order for 5,000 units at $24.15 each. Variable cost is $15 per unit. What contribution would the order earn?

Savanna Fresh Ltd normally sells at $20 per unit. Variable cost is $12 per unit and fixed cost per unit at current output is $3. It has a capacity of 20,000 units and currently produces 11,000. A customer offers to buy 5,000 units at $15.75 each. Calculate the contribution from the order.
items.answer: Contribution $18,750
items.markingKey: Contribution per unit = $15.75 − $12 = $3.75; total = $18,750 [2]. [2]

items.stem: Tejo Mobility SA normally sells at $40 per unit. Variable cost is $20 per unit and fixed cost per unit at current output is $6. It has a capacity of 25,000 units and currently produces 16,000. A customer offers to buy 5,000 units at $28.60 each. Calculate the contribution from the order and explain why the order is acceptable even though the price is close to full cost ($26).
items.answer: Contribution $43,000
items.markingKey: Contribution per unit = $28.60 − $20 = $8.60; total = $43,000 [2]; fixed costs are already covered by existing output, so extra contribution adds to profit [1]. [3]

items.stem: Define the term 'budget'.
items.answer: A detailed financial plan for a future period, setting targets for revenue, costs or other items, agreed in advance.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, a detailed financial plan for a future period, setting targets for revenue, costs or other items, agreed in advance. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain two benefits of using budgets.
items.answer: They set targets that guide and motivate managers; they help coordinate departments and control spending through variance analysis.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark benefit, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Explain why a flexible budget gives a better basis for variance analysis than a fixed budget.
items.answer: If output differs from plan, a fixed budget's costs are not comparable; flexing to actual output shows whether costs were controlled efficiently.
items.markingKey: 1 mark output differences; 1 mark fair comparison. [2]

items.answer: Points to develop for Andes Textil: adverse revenue variance means revenue below budget; lower sales volume because of competition or economy; lower prices or discounts; unrealistic budget in the first place.

items.stem: Which of the following best defines 'contribution costing'?
options: The extra cost of producing one more unit of output, usually equal to the variable cost per unit.
A variance that increases profit compared with the budget, e.g. actual revenue above budget or actual costs below budget.
A one-off order from a customer, often at a lower price than normal, which the business must decide whether to accept.
A costing method that charges only variable (direct) costs to products; the contribution each product makes towards fixed costs and profit is calculated.
items.answer: A costing method that charges only variable (direct) costs to products; the contribution each product makes towards fixed costs and profit is calculated.
items.markingKey: contribution costing: A costing method that charges only variable (direct) costs to products; the contribution each product makes towards fixed costs and profit is calculated.

items.stem: A global brand has threatened to cancel its contract after a report on long working hours. items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why contribution costing is useful for short-term decisions. (b) Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of full costing.
